title: The silent teacher under the banyan
hookLine: under a banyan tree, old students sit before a young teacher who says nothing, and their doubts are gone
carry: chin mudra: the small self meets the great
tomorrow: Why is breath more than air?

cards: How strange, an old Sanskrit verse begins. Under a banyan tree sit the students, and they are old. Their teacher is young.
And the teacher's lecture is silence. Yet the students' doubts are cut away. The teacher in that verse is Dakshinamurti, Shiva as the teacher.
In images of him beneath the tree, one hand is raised, and in that hand the thumb and the first finger touch to make a small circle. He doesn't explain it. In the verse, the silence is enough.

teach.b: The shape is simple. The tip of the index finger meets the tip of the thumb. The other three fingers stay straight, relaxed.

It's called chin mudra, the seal of consciousness, or jnana mudra, the seal of knowledge. Lineages use the two names a little differently, sometimes by whether the palm faces up or down, but the finger shape is the same.

Teachers read the shape like a sentence. In one common reading, the thumb stands for the Supreme, Brahman. The index finger, the one we point with, stands for the individual self, always pointing outward at this and that.

teach.h: THE SMALL SELF BENDS TO THE GREAT.
teach.b: When the index finger bends and touches the thumb, the small self meets the great one.

teach.h: THREE FINGERS: GUNAS, OR THREE STATES.
teach.b: And the three fingers left standing? Some teachers say they are the three gunas, the qualities that make up the world.

Others say they are the three states this path spent time with not long ago: waking, dreaming, deep sleep. Either way, in that reading the circle is made apart from the three, and the meeting happens beyond them.
That's why it suits Dakshinamurti. Some readers say the students are old because they've studied everything and heard every argument. What finally answers them isn't another argument.
It's a hand, held still, showing the meeting instead of describing it. The Taittiriya Upanishad says something similar about its own subject: it's where words turn back, unable to reach it.
In the verse's picture, the silence isn't because there's nothing to say, but because this is something better shown.
And the hand can show it on a meditation seat, palm resting on the knee, as easily as under a banyan tree.

how: Practitioners sit in meditation with chin or jnana mudra, thumb and index finger touching and the hands resting on the knees; images of Dakshinamurti show him seated beneath a banyan tree with his hand in this mudra.

o: the silent vows kept by students of a teacher
hand seals, like thumb and finger joined in a circle
a teacher's spoken lessons under a banyan tree

games.q: the seal of consciousness — tap the pairs.
p: Shiva as the teacher, under a banyan

s: in the verse, Dakshinamurti answers his students with a long lecture
the verse says his lecture is silence, and their doubts are cut away.
in chin mudra the tips of the thumb and index finger touch
the other three fingers stay straight and relaxed.
every lineage reads the three standing fingers the same way
some say the three gunas, others the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep.

games.q: you're one of the old students under the banyan tree. your young teacher sits with one hand raised and says nothing. what happens?
o: you leave to find a teacher who talks.
you start explaining it to each other.
games.why: the verse says the teacher's lecture is silence, and the students' doubts are cut away. The hand shows what words couldn't.

practice: Sit upright, rest the backs of the hands on the knees or thighs, and let the tip of each index finger meet the tip of the thumb, lightly, the other three fingers straight but soft.
Let the breath settle and say nothing, even inside. If thoughts start explaining, let them go and come back to the touch of the two fingertips.

wordCard.voice: The mudras. Today, chin mudra, the seal of consciousness: thumb and first finger joined, read by teachers as the small self bowing to the great, shown in silence.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: chinmudra, the seal of consciousness. Thumb and index finger joined, as Dakshinamurti holds it.
